food.text: Ancient Carthage sat on the coast of what is now Tunisia. Its strategic location gave it access to abundant fertile land and to major maritime trade routes that reached West Asia and Northern Europe. Farmland and sea trade helped make it one of the ancient world's richest cities.

Berbers had food staples such as figs, olives and dates, and they often prepared lamb and poultry dishes. These foods are still used in abundance in Moroccan cuisine. The Berber culture underneath later influences is described as multi-millennial, reaching back to prehistoric times.

Tunisian cuisine consists of cooking traditions developed in Tunisia since antiquity. It is described as a blend of Arab, Mediterranean, Punic and Berber cooking. It developed from Berbers, ancient Carthage, Rome, the Islamic conquest of the Maghreb and the Ottoman Empire.

Olive trees in Algeria have a long history dating back to ancient times. Today the country has many olive groves, especially in its northern and coastal regions, where the climate and soil suit olive cultivation. Olives remain a key ingredient in dishes such as the Algerian tajine zitoun.

The Greek author Diodorus Siculus, who had access to ancient writings that were later lost, described the agricultural land near the city of Carthage around 310 BC. His account preserves a glimpse of the farmland surrounding the Carthaginian capital.

art.text: Carthage absorbed gods from Greece, Egypt, Mesopotamia and Italy, and its art reflected this. The Egyptian god Bes, worshipped for warding off evil spirits, is featured prominently in Punic mausoleums.

Julius Caesar rebuilt Carthage between 49 and 44 BC as Colonia Iulia Concordia Carthago. By the first century it was the second-largest city in the western Roman Empire, and an amphitheatre was among its major monuments.

Henna, a reddish dye made from the dried leaves of Lawsonia inermis, has been used for body art since at least antiquity. It is said to originate in North Africa, including the Maghreb, and its use spread to Carthage among other places.

Carthage had a temple to Isis, the Egyptian goddess whose cult spread across the Mediterranean. A well preserved sarcophagus from the city depicts one of her priestesses in Hellenistic style, mixing Egyptian religion with Greek artistic fashion.

French-led excavations at Carthage began in 1921. René Dussaud identified a 4th-century BC stela found there as depicting a child sacrifice. The excavations of the 1920s first drew attention because of the evidence they produced for child sacrifice, though scholars still disagree over whether Carthage practiced it.

The 5th-century bishop Victor Vitensis recorded that the Vandals destroyed parts of Carthage, including various buildings and churches. The Vandals conquered the city in 439 and made it their capital for a century. Once in power they persecuted the ecclesiastical authorities, taxed the locals aggressively and routinely launched naval raids on Romans in the Mediterranean.

Cyprian was beheaded by the sword at Carthage on 14 September 258 AD, after he removed his garments without assistance, knelt down, prayed and blindfolded himself. Christians buried his body near the place of execution, and churches were later erected over his tomb and over the place where he died. In later centuries the Vandals destroyed these churches.

Excavators in 1994 to 2000 studied a building of Roman Carthage that stood against the theater and was built entirely above ground level. It had semi-circular corridors for the circulation of visitors, and Tertullian mentions burial sites being discovered during its construction.

war.text: The Punic Wars were fought between the Roman Republic and the Carthaginian Empire from 264 to 146 BC. Three wars made up forty-three years of fighting on land and sea across the western Mediterranean. At the start Carthage was the dominant power, while Rome had a strong army but no navy. The last war ended in 146 BC, when the Romans stormed Carthage, sacked it, slaughtered or enslaved its population and completely demolished the city; the 50,000 prisoners taken were sold into slavery.

The Battle of Zama in 202 BC, fought in what is now Tunisia, ended the Second Punic War. Scipio Africanus led about 40,000 Romans against Hannibal's Carthaginians, who fielded 40,000 or 50,000 men and 80 war elephants. When the Roman cavalry returned and charged the Carthaginian infantry in the rear, their line collapsed and there was a great massacre. Polybius states that 20,000 Carthaginians were killed and as many again taken prisoner, against 1,500 Romans killed, and the defeat was so severe that Carthage capitulated and Hannibal was forced into exile.

In 149 BC the Carthaginians tried to appease a large Roman army that had landed at Utica, and surrendered all of their weapons, including 200,000 sets of armour and 2,000 catapults according to surviving records. Their warships sailed to Utica and were burnt in the harbour. Once Carthage was disarmed, the consuls demanded that the Carthaginians abandon their city and move 16 kilometres from the sea, so that Carthage could be destroyed. The Carthaginians broke off negotiations and prepared to defend the city, and the Romans besieged it for nearly three years.

In 241 BC the Mercenary War began over wages owed to 20,000 foreign soldiers who had fought for Carthage in Sicily. The army mutinied under Spendius and Matho, and 70,000 Africans from Carthage's oppressed dependent territories joined them. Carthage fared poorly in the early fighting.

The peace treaty that ended the Second Punic War stripped Carthage of all of its overseas territories and some of its African ones. It required an indemnity of 10,000 silver talents over 50 years, and hostages were taken. Carthage was forbidden to possess war elephants, its fleet was limited to 10 warships, and it was prohibited from waging war outside Africa, and in Africa only with Rome's permission.

After the Second Punic War, Carthage could wage war in Africa only with Rome's express permission. Masinissa of Numidia exploited this to raid and seize Carthaginian land with impunity, and in 151 BC Carthage sent an army under Hasdrubal against him anyway. The Battle of Oroscopa ended in disaster and the surrender of the Carthaginian army, and many Carthaginians were then massacred by the Numidians. Hasdrubal escaped to Carthage, where he was condemned to death in an attempt to placate Rome, while anti-Carthaginian factions in Rome used the episode as a pretext for a punitive expedition.

After Scipio's army landed near the Carthaginian port of Utica, the Carthaginians and their Numidian allies were repeatedly beaten in battle. In a night attack Scipio's men set fire to the Numidians' reed barracks, and in the panic the Numidians were dispersed with heavy casualties. The Romans then attacked the surprised Carthaginians in the dark and again inflicted heavy casualties. The Roman ally Masinissa became the leading Numidian ruler. Scipio and Carthage then entered peace negotiations, and Carthage recalled Hannibal from Italy.

When Scipio Aemilianus took command at Carthage, he tightened the siege and began building a large mole to stop blockade runners from bringing supplies into the city. Frustrated at the amount of food being shipped in, he sought to cut off access to the harbour. The Romans later built a large brick structure in the harbour area that dominated the city wall. After Scipio withdrew from a night assault, Hasdrubal had Roman prisoners tortured to death on the walls in view of the Roman army, to harden the citizens' will to resist. He then put to death members of the city council who denounced him and took full control of the city.

During the Mercenary War, Hamilcar Barca at first treated captured rebels well, offering them a choice of joining his army or free passage home, in an attempt to woo the rebels over. To remove any chance of goodwill between the sides, Spendius, encouraged by Autaritus, had 700 Carthaginian prisoners, including Gisco, tortured to death: their hands were cut off, they were castrated, their legs were broken, and they were thrown into a pit and buried alive. Hamilcar killed his prisoners in turn, and any later prisoners the Carthaginians took were trampled to death by elephants.

After Carthage crushed the mercenary revolt, it prepared to reoccupy Sardinia, where mutinous soldiers had killed their officers and the governor, and then slaughtered all the Carthaginians on the island. Rome declared that reoccupation would be an act of war and occupied both Sardinia and Corsica. This has been considered the single greatest cause of the Second Punic War breaking out in 218 BC.

During the siege of Carthage, the Carthaginians had partially rebuilt their fleet, and it sortied to the Romans' surprise. After an indecisive engagement, a collision blocked the new channel while the Carthaginian ships were pinned against the city's sea wall. With no room to manoeuvre, the Romans sank or captured many of them before the survivors escaped back into harbour. When the Romans then advanced on the harbour defences, Carthaginians swam across at night and set fire to several siege engines, and many legionaries panicked and fled. Scipio had his mounted bodyguard attack the fleeing legionaries when they disregarded his orders to halt.

The main source for the Third Punic War is Polybius, a Greek sent to Rome in 167 BC as a hostage. He accompanied Scipio Aemilianus during the North African campaign and personally interviewed participants from both sides. His works include a now-lost manual on military tactics.

literature.text: Almost nothing written in Phoenician or Punic survives directly. The language of Ancient Carthage is known from inscriptions, coins, and Greek and Latin sources, such as fragments of Mago's agricultural treatise, a Greek translation of Hanno the Navigator's voyage, and a few lines in Plautus's Poenulus.

Publius Terentius Afer, known as Terence, was a Berber born in Carthage (195–159 BC). In Rome he mastered the Latin language and became a celebrated Roman playwright. The pro-Hellenic Scipio circle welcomed and embraced him.

Juba II, a Berber king and husband of Cleopatra's daughter, was also a scholar and an author in Greek of no less than nine works. He wrote for the Mediterranean-wide audience enjoying classical literature. His Libyka, a work on North Africa, survives only in fragments quoted by other ancient authors.

Virgil's epic poem the Aeneid, published around 19 BC, is the best source for Dido's story. She is a clever queen who founded Carthage after fleeing her tyrannical brother. When Aeneas leaves, Dido cannot bear to live: she has her sister Anna build a pyre, climbs onto it, lies on the couch she called their bridal bed, and stabs herself with Aeneas' sword.

Greco-Roman sources mention a number of Punic books saved from the looting and burning of Carthage by the legions of Scipio Aemilianus in the spring of 146 BC. According to Pliny, after the fall of Carthage many of these books were handed over to the Numidian rulers. The Roman Senate ordered only one text translated into Latin: Mago's agricultural treatise. It set up a commission led by Decimus Junius Piso.

Some of Hiempsal II's libri punici probably escaped the fires that consumed Carthage in 146 BC. They likely wound up in the large royal library of his grandson Juba II, and would have been useful to him when composing his Libyka.

The oldest references to Dido come from the lost writings of the Sicilian historian Timaeus of Tauromenium. In his Histories, he claims that Dido founded Carthage in 814 BC, around the same time as the founding of Rome.

Around 190 BC the popular dramatist Plautus wrote the Roman comedy Poenulus, meaning 'The Carthaginian'. It featured an extended family from Carthage who, in Greece, triumphed over the nefarious schemes of a leno, a Roman slaver.

Among the documents saved from fallen Carthage may have been the five-centuries-old 'log book' of Hanno the Navigator, called the Periplus. It may have been Juba II who 'discovered' it in the royal library.

According to Polybius and Titus Livy, Hannibal had his deeds recorded in Phoenician and Greek in 205 BC, in the temple of Hera in Lacinia. This was probably the continuation of an ancient tradition in which Carthaginian generals wrote down their heroic deeds and gave them to a temple to be preserved.

A fragment of an epic poem by Gnaeus Naevius, who died at Utica in 201 BC, includes a passage that might be part of a conversation between Aeneas and Dido. It is unknown who first combined Dido's story with the tradition connecting Aeneas to Rome.

Juba II was a Berber king, husband of Cleopatra's daughter, and the author in Greek of no less than nine works, including Libyka on North Africa. Some Carthaginian libri punici that escaped the fires of 146 BC probably reached his library. He may have discovered the five-centuries-old log book of Hanno the Navigator, called the Periplus.

Krahmalkov reads a few Punic-language inscriptions as poetry, remnants of a tradition of rhymed rhetorical prose and iambic poetry. His text and translation are harshly disputed, however. Other scholars call his analysis of the Iulius Nasif inscription 'preposterous' and 'misrepresentative'.

science.text: The Baths of Antoninus in Carthage are the largest set of Roman thermae built on the African continent, and one of the three largest in the Roman Empire. They were built under Emperor Hadrian and named after the emperor who followed him, Antoninus Pius.

Mago of Carthage wrote a huge agricultural manual in Punic, divided into 28 books. It recorded the farming knowledge of Carthage, drawing on local Berber and Punic traditional practices, including veterinary knowledge.
Eratosthenes, a mathematician, geographer and astronomer from Cyrene, became librarian at the Library of Alexandria. He is credited as the first person to calculate the circumference of the Earth.

Apuleius, born in Madauros in Numidia, was accused of using charms and magic spells to win the affections and fortune of a wealthy widow, Pudentilla. In his defence, the Apologia, he argued that his supposed magical operations were really indispensable scientific experiments, like those of Aristotle and Hippocrates. He also accused an extravagant personal enemy of turning his own house into a brothel and prostituting his wife.

The clay soil beside the Mediterranean meant the Baths of Antoninus needed a larger foundation. Roman bathhouses usually had service areas in the basement, but the soft clay could not support them. The designers adapted by raising the structure, which made these baths taller than other Roman bathhouses.

Rome destroyed Carthage in 146 BC, and afterwards the Carthaginian libraries were given to the kings of Numidia. Mago's farming book was uniquely the one work retrieved and brought to Rome. The Roman Senate paid for D. Junius Silanus to translate it in full into Latin.

Mago, the Carthaginian agronomist, wrote on viticulture, and his works were translated from Punic into Latin. Later Roman writers such as Columella quoted him. Wine production in Tunisia was probably introduced by the Phoenicians when Carthage was established.

Cyrene exported silphium, a medicinal plant, and this trade helped make the Battiad dynasty of rulers rich and powerful. Along with horses, it was a source of the city's wealth from the late seventh century BC.

Juba II, a Berber king, was also a scholar who wrote at least nine works in Greek, including Libyka on North Africa. He may have discovered the five-century-old log book of Hanno the Navigator, called the Periplus, among documents saved from fallen Carthage.
The Baths of Antoninus were part of a Roman hydraulic complex linking Zaghouan and Carthage. On 17 February 2012, the Tunisian government proposed this complex as a future World Heritage site.
Mago's manual was also adapted into Greek by Cassius Dionysius. That Greek version was later shortened by Diophanes of Nicaea into six books, showing how far Carthaginian farming knowledge travelled.
Apuleius wrote technical treatises that have not survived. They covered subjects including medicine, natural history, astronomy, agriculture, music and arithmetic.

politics.text: Some ancient sources, such as Philistos of Syracuse, place Carthage's founding at an early date of around 1215 BC, before the fall of Troy in 1180 BC. The Sicilian Greek historian Timaeus instead dated it to 814 BC, the date generally accepted by modern historians.

Carthage was settled around 814 BC by merchants from Tyre, then became independent after Phoenicia fell to the Neo-Assyrian Empire in the 7th century BC. By 300 BC it controlled the coast of northwestern Africa, parts of Iberia, and the islands of Sicily, Sardinia, Corsica, Malta and the Balearics.

Carthage and the emerging Roman Republic fought a long conflict known as the Punic Wars, lasting from 264 to 146 BC. In 146 BC Rome finally destroyed Carthage. A Roman Carthage was later established on the ruins of the first.

In 44 CE the Roman Empire incorporated the Berber kingdom of Mauretania in the western Maghreb as a province. It was later divided into Mauretania Caesariensis and Mauretania Tingitana. The area around Carthage was already part of Africa Proconsularis, and Roman rule was effective as the provinces became integrated into the empire.

After Rome conquered Carthage, Utica became the regional capital. Its harbour sat at the outlet of the Medjerda River, but grain cultivation in the Tunisian mountains sent large amounts of silt down the river. The silt built up until the harbour was useless, so Rome looked for a new harbour town.

Tradition credits Queen Elissa, or Dido, of Tyre with founding Carthage, though her historicity has been questioned. In the myth, a local tribe offered her as much land as an oxhide could cover, so she cut the hide into strips to mark out the city's perimeter. As Carthage prospered, it sent colonists abroad and magistrates to rule the colonies.

Mago I ruled Carthage from 550 BC to 530 BC and founded the Magonid dynasty. He began as a general, and under him Carthage became the dominant Phoenician military power in the western Mediterranean. One of his political achievements was an alliance with the Etruscans against the Greeks.

Rome rebuilt Carthage under Julius Caesar between 49 and 44 BC, naming it Colonia Iulia Concordia Carthago. By the first century it was the second-largest city in the western half of the Roman Empire. It was the centre of the province of Africa, a major breadbasket of the empire.

Even at the height of Carthaginian power, not every part of its territory was ruled directly. Tripoli remained de facto autonomous under local Libyco-Phoenicians, a mixed people of Libyans (specifically Macae) and Phoenicians, who paid only nominal tribute.

Between 540 and 535 BC, a Carthaginian-Etruscan alliance expelled the Greeks from Corsica after the Battle of Alalia. The Etruscans took control of Corsica, while Carthage concentrated on Sardinia to make sure no Greek presence would be established there.

The Vandals ruled much of the area after Rome fell, but their army was not a standing army and weakened under later kings from Huneric to Gelimer. No frontier army guarded against the Mauri, who encroached on the kingdom's borders and kept the interior under Berber control.

Two failed attempts by Majorian and Basiliscus to recapture Carthage came in the 5th century. Then the Eastern Roman Empire used Gelimer's deposition of Gaiseric's grandson Hilderic as a casus belli. Belisarius made his formal entry into Carthage in October 533, ending the Vandal Kingdom.

In 525 BC the Phoenicians refused to lend ships to the Persian king Cambyses for an African expedition. Carthage may thereby have been spared a trial of arms against the Persian Empire. It may also have paid tribute irregularly to the Great King.

In the late 170s or 180s, during the reign of Commodus, Mauri raiders crossed into the Roman province of Baetica and besieged the town of Singilia Barba. Roman troops from the province of Mauretania Tingitana, led by C. Vallius Maximianus, freed the town from the siege.

In the mid-first century AD, Roman authorities launched an extensive surveying campaign around Cyrene. Its aim was to reclaim public land that had slipped into private control and stopped paying dividends to the treasury.

philosophy.text: The Carthaginians had a high degree of religious syncretism, taking in deities and practices from Greece, Egypt, Mesopotamia and Italy. Many of their own cults and practices in turn spread across the Mediterranean through trade and colonisation.

Punic religion suffused society, with no stark distinction between religious and secular spheres. No literary sources survive, so it is reconstructed mainly from inscriptions and archaeological evidence. An important sacred space was the tophet, a large open air sanctuary where urns of cremated infants and animals were buried, and Greco-Roman and biblical sources describe children being sacrificed by burning, though scholars debate whether this happened.

Among Berber communities where agriculture was possible, rain and water sources played important parts in belief systems. Worship of spirits living in caverns and grottos was common, and the cavern-related fertility goddess Ifru was widespread in coastal Algeria.

From at least the sixth century BC, Melqart was increasingly identified with the Greek Heracles and revered by both Greeks and Carthaginians. An inscription in Malta honors him in both Greek and Punic, and he became a unifying figure among Carthage's allies in the wars against Rome.
After the Roman Republic conquered Punic regions in the third and second centuries BC, Punic religious practices continued. In some cases they survived until the fourth century AD.

Punic sacrifices had to follow strict specifications, set out on nine surviving inscriptions called sacrificial tariffs. The longest, KAI 69, the Marseille Tariff, probably stood in Carthage and lists the portions that priests of a temple of Baal Saphon could claim.

In the early 3rd century CE, a large Jewish necropolis at Gammarth near Carthage held 105 chambers, each with roughly 15 loculi, the burial niches for the dead. Together they would have allowed burial for 1500 people. The French archaeologist Alfred Louis Delattre uncovered it. Symbols of the Temple menorah, shofar, lulav and etrog prove its Jewishness, yet the inscriptions are mostly in Latin.
philosophy.source_title: History of the Jews in Carthage

philosophy.text: French-led excavations at Carthage began in 1921, and from 1923 they reported a large quantity of urns containing a mixture of animal and children's bones. René Dussaud identified a 4th-century BC stela found in Carthage as depicting a child sacrifice. Some scholars believed the mix of children's and animal bones, with inscriptions mentioning mlk, showed that child sacrifice was common practice in Carthage, but others argued the site held only children's cemeteries, and the article notes that the bones indicate the infants were not sacrificed.

A tradition among the Jews of Djerba says their community was built of exiles after the Siege of Jerusalem in 597 BCE, and that the el Ghriba Synagogue is equally ancient. Yet the earliest evidence of Jewish presence in the area dates to the 2nd century CE.
philosophy.source_title: History of the Jews in Carthage

culture.text: The Carthaginians borrowed gods freely from the cultures they met, including Greece, Egypt, Mesopotamia and Italy. Their cults and practices also spread across the Mediterranean through trade and colonisation. Carthage had communities of Jews, Greeks, Romans and Libyans.

According to legend, Dido asked a local tribe for land and was told she could have as much as an oxhide could cover. She cut the oxhide into strips and used them to lay out the perimeter of her new city, Carthage.

Traditional Berber belief in the Maghreb was tied to nature. In farming areas rain and water sources mattered, and people worshipped spirits living in caverns and grottos. In pastoral areas such as Libya, the sun and moon were commonly worshipped, and Berber groups also practiced ancestor worship.

The Egyptian god Bes was popular in Carthage for warding off evil spirits and appears prominently in Punic mausoleums. Isis also had a temple in Carthage. A well preserved sarcophagus shows one of her priestesses in Hellenistic style.

Melqart was increasingly identified with the Greek Heracles and was revered by both Greeks and Carthaginians. He became popular enough to serve as a unifying figure among Carthage's allies in the wars against Rome. His awakening rite may have persisted in Numidia as late as the second century AD.

Large open air sanctuaries known as tophets were important sacred spaces in Punic religion. Urns holding the cremated bones of infants and animals were buried there, and uneven burning on the bones shows they were burned on an open air pyre. Greco-Roman and biblical sources describe the Carthaginians sacrificing children by burning, and the discovery of the Carthage tophet in 1921, with its urns of cremated children, seemed to confirm this. Scholars still debate whether, and how far, child sacrifice occurred; some hold that all the remains were sacrificed, others only some.

Since 1982, French archaeologist Serge Lancel has excavated a residential area of Punic Carthage on Byrsa hill. The neighborhood dates to the early second century BC. Its houses, shops and private spaces reveal daily life in Punic Carthage.

The Berber calendar, called Yennayer, is an agricultural calendar. Its starting point is the year 950 BCE, which roughly marks the rise to the Egyptian throne of the Amazigh (Meshwesh) Pharaoh Sheshonq I. In Morocco it is celebrated on January 14.

Punic sacrifices had to follow strict specifications, set out on nine surviving inscriptions known as sacrificial tariffs. The longest, the Marseille Tariff, probably originally stood in Carthage. It lists the portions of sacrifices that the priests of a temple of Baal Saphon were entitled to.

Carthage kept sending annual tribute to its mother city Tyre for the temple of Melqart, at irregular intervals, over the centuries. This continued even after Carthage was probably politically independent. It shows how religious ties outlasted political ones.

A stele erected at Carthage in the mid-second century BC by a woman named Abibaal shows the sacrifice of a cow's head by burning on an altar. The details of the image show continuity with much earlier Near Eastern sacrificial rituals. Many Punic tophet inscriptions call their own sacrificial ritual mlk, which some scholars connect with the biblical Moloch, to whom the Hebrew Bible says children were burned.
